title: LLM Inference Learning Series: Running a Local LLM Server Before Moving to GPUs
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: Lab 1 — Running a Local LLM Server
In the previous articles of this series, I talked about core LLM inference concepts: latency, throughput, TTFT, ITL, batching, concurrency, prompt processing, decode cost, and system utilization.
Now it is time to make those ideas measurable.
This is the first hands-on lab in the series, and I intentionally started local.

For this lab, I used a Mac setup with llama.cpp. The lab is designed for Apple Silicon, but the same learning pattern can run on CPU-only setups as well. It may be slower, and your numbers will be different, but the concepts remain the same.
The goal of this first lab is not to build the fastest inference server. The goal is to understand what actually happens when we run a local model, send real requests, and measure the behavior.
You can follow the full lab here:
GitHub Lab: https://github.com/aruanurag/llm-inference-lab/tree/main/labs/01-local-llm-serving-apple-silicon
Why start local?
Before moving to vLLM, cloud GPUs, managed inference endpoints, Kubernetes, autoscaling, and cost optimization, I wanted a simple baseline where the moving parts are visible.
This first lab uses:

A local machine.
A small quantized GGUF model.
llama.cpp as the runtime.
An OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint.
A benchmark script to measure inference metrics.
Simple system tools to observe CPU, memory, and GPU activity.

This gives us a controlled starting point. Later in the series, I will move to vLLM and cloud environments where GPU access is easier and more cost-efficient. I may also start with simple CPU-based cloud runs before moving to GPU, just to keep the comparisons clean.
Runtime choice: llama.cpp
For Lab 1, I used llama.cpp.
Why?

It works well on Apple Silicon.
It supports Metal acceleration.
It runs quantized GGUF models.
It exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API.
It is simple enough for a first reproducible lab.
Once the server is running, requests go to:
http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions

That is useful because the client-side benchmarking flow can stay familiar even when the backend changes later. Today it is llama.cpp; in future labs, it can be vLLM or a cloud-hosted inference endpoint.
Model choice: start small
For the first run, I used:
Qwen2.5 1.5B Instruct, Q4_K_M
This is not about using the smartest model. It is about using a model that starts reliably, fits comfortably, and lets us focus on inference behavior.
Good first model choices for this lab include:

Qwen2.5 1.5B Instruct GGUF, Q4 or Q5.
Llama 3.2 1B or 3B Instruct GGUF, Q4 or Q5.
Phi-3 Mini GGUF, Q4, if memory allows.
The first rule of inference labs: make the first experiment reproducible before making it impressive.
What this lab measures
This lab focuses on the same metrics we discussed in the earlier inference articles.
Core latency metrics:

TTFT: time to first token.
Approximate ITL: time between streamed output chunks.
End-to-end latency: total time from request start to completed response.
Throughput metrics:

Output tokens per second.
Requests per second.
Approximate total tokens per second.
System behavior:

Startup time.
CPU usage.
Memory usage.
GPU / Metal activity.
Concurrency level.
Batch size.
Micro-batch size.
p50, p95, and p99 latency.
These metrics will continue to matter as the labs move from local serving to GPU-backed serving.
Lab flow
The lab follows a simple sequence:

Set up llama.cpp.
Download a small GGUF model.
Start a local llama-server.
Verify the server health endpoint.
Send one OpenAI-compatible chat request.
Run benchmark experiments.
Observe CPU, memory, and GPU behavior.
Change batching settings.
Collect and compare results.
Visualize the benchmark outputs.
This is the basic habit I want to build in the series: change one thing, measure again, and compare.
Experiment 1: Single request, short prompt, short output
The first experiment sends one short prompt and asks for a short response.
Example:
Explain KV cache in two sentences.
This establishes the baseline.
The main question is:
How long does the server take to produce the first token?
This is where TTFT becomes real. It is no longer just a definition. You can actually see the delay before the first streamed chunk arrives.
This matters because users often judge responsiveness by the time it takes for the first token to appear, not only by the total completion time.
Experiment 2: Long prompt, short output
The second experiment keeps the output short but increases the prompt length.
This helps isolate prefill cost.
In transformer inference, the model has to process the input prompt before it can generate the next token. So longer prompts usually increase the amount of work before generation starts.
The question here is:
Does TTFT increase when the prompt gets longer?
This is especially important for real-world applications like:

RAG systems with retrieved documents.
Chat applications with long conversation history.
Agents with tool outputs.
Code assistants with large context.
Enterprise assistants with policy, ticket, or document context.
Even if the final answer is short, the prompt can be long. That means the user may still experience high TTFT.
Experiment 3: Short prompt, long output
The third experiment does the opposite.
The prompt is short, but the output length is increased.
Example:
Write a compact tutorial on continuous batching.
Now the goal is to observe decode cost.
The question becomes:
Does end-to-end latency increase mostly because more output tokens are generated?
This is why max token settings matter so much in production. They are not just safety limits. They directly affect latency, capacity, and cost.
Two requests can have similar TTFT but very different end-to-end latency if one generates 50 tokens and the other generates 500.
Experiment 4: Multiple concurrent requests
After single-request testing, the lab adds concurrency.
Example:

concurrency = 4
requests = 12
Now we are no longer testing only one request. We are testing serving behavior under load.
The important questions are:

Does throughput improve?
What happens to p50 latency?
What happens to p95 latency?
Does approximate ITL get worse?
Does the server remain stable?

This is where inference tradeoffs become visible. A system may produce better throughput with concurrency, but tail latency can get worse because requests are competing for the same compute resources.
That tradeoff will become even more important in later labs with vLLM, continuous batching, and GPU-backed serving.
Experiment 5: Batch size and micro-batch size
The final experiment changes server-side batching knobs in llama.cpp.
The two knobs are:

BATCH_SIZE: logical batch size. This affects how much prompt work the server tries to process together.
UBATCH_SIZE: physical micro-batch size. This controls how that work is split into smaller chunks.
The lab compares a conservative setting:

BATCH_SIZE=256
UBATCH_SIZE=64
with a larger setting:

BATCH_SIZE=1024
UBATCH_SIZE=256
The benchmark stays the same. Only the server configuration changes.
The questions are:

Did TTFT improve or get worse?
Did p95 latency improve or get worse?
Did throughput improve?
Did memory usage change?
Did the server become unstable?
This is the important lesson: there is no universal best batch size. The right value depends on model size, context size, memory, hardware, runtime, and concurrency.
Guessing is not enough. You have to measure.
CPU, GPU, and Metal observation
Another part of the lab is watching the machine while inference is running.
On macOS, I used tools like:

top
ps
Activity Monitor
powermetrics
The goal is not perfect profiling yet. The goal is to connect inference metrics with system behavior.
Things to observe:

Is CPU usage high?
How much memory is the server using?
Does Activity Monitor show GPU activity?
Do startup logs mention Metal?
What happens with CPU-only mode?
What changes when Metal offload is enabled?
In this lab, GPU_LAYERS controls offload behavior:

GPU_LAYERS=0      -> CPU-only
GPU_LAYERS=auto   -> let llama.cpp decide Metal offload
GPU_LAYERS=all    -> try to offload all possible layers

This habit will matter even more later in cloud GPU labs. Having a GPU does not automatically mean the system is efficient. We still need to understand utilization, memory pressure, batching behavior, and latency.
Failure is also a valid result
The lab includes a place to record failures.
If something fails, record:

Exact command.
Exact error.
Machine type.
Model file.
What you tried next.
This is useful because inference work often starts with constraints:

This model does not fit.
This quantization is not stable.
This runtime setting does not work on this machine.
This batch size causes memory pressure.
This offload mode does not behave as expected.
A good inference experiment does not only collect successful benchmark numbers. It also collects limits.
Why this lab matters
This first lab is small by design.
But it creates the foundation for everything that comes next.
From here, we can change one layer at a time:

Move from llama.cpp to vLLM.
Move from local CPU or Metal acceleration to cloud GPU.
Compare prompt-heavy workloads with decode-heavy workloads.
Study continuous batching more directly.
Observe KV cache behavior.
Explore concurrency limits.
Compare cost per request.
Compare latency under different serving configurations.
The infrastructure will become more advanced, but the measurement mindset will stay the same:

Start with a question.
Run a controlled experiment.
Measure TTFT, ITL, latency, throughput, and utilization.
Change one thing.
Measure again.
That is how inference stops being a black box.
Final thought
It is tempting to start LLM inference learning with the biggest model and the fastest GPU available.
But for learning, that is not always the best first step.
A small local lab can teach the fundamentals clearly:

You see the server start.
You see the model load.
You send the request.
You watch the first token.
You increase the prompt.
You increase the output.
You add concurrency.
You change batching.
You observe CPU, memory, and GPU behavior.
And suddenly, the metrics from earlier articles are no longer theoretical. They are measurements from a real system.
That is the goal of Lab 1:
Start local. Measure carefully. Build intuition. Then scale.
